title: Climate migrations
subtitle: 216 million displaced by 2050?
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: The climate will force hundreds of millions of people from their homes, but no international law yet protects them.

hero.hook: Climate already drives out more people than war, but no law knows what to call them.

blocks.text: A rise in water levels does not always announce itself with a spectacular wave: it first eats up a field, then a well, then an entire village. Elsewhere, extreme heat makes the air almost impossible to breathe. In both cases, entire families must leave, not because of war, but because of the climate. These forced departures have a name: **climatic migrations**. The problem is that no international law really recognizes them.

sections.title: An exodus already bigger than the war

blocks.text: In **2022**, one figure marked a turning point: climate disasters caused **60 million internal displacements**, forced departures within a country itself. For the first time, this number exceeded that of people fleeing wars.
In **2009**, the government of  held a council of ministers underwater, in oxygen tanks and diving suits, to alert the world about the possible disappearance of this archipelago. [[Maldives]]

blocks.caption: Migrants are crossing the Mediterranean: the climate crisis is now added to political crises as a driving force behind departures.

blocks.text: The rest looks more worrying: the **World Bank** estimates that without massive effort, climate change could force **216 million people** to migrate by **2050**. In Bangladesh, the ocean is eating away at agricultural land; in sub-Saharan Africa, there is a shortage of water; in the Pacific, certain island states risk the total disappearance of their territory.

sections.title: Two speeds of rupture: shock and wear

blocks.text: There are two ways that climate drives out populations. **sudden disasters**, like storms, cause sudden but often temporary departures, before the inhabitants' ability to bounce back is exhausted through repetition. **slow degradation** transforms a territory forever: rising water levels make the soils salty, killing crops before the water even reaches homes, while desertification gradually changes pastures into barren lands, pushing nomadic communities towards  or exile in the city. [[forced sedentary lifestyle]]

A new threat worries scientists: **humid heat**. When temperature and humidity exceed a certain threshold, the body can no longer cool itself by sweating. By 2050, parts of the Persian Gulf or South Asia could become deadly for anyone who stays outside for more than a few hours.

sections.title: A legal vacuum in the face of a global crisis

blocks.text: Despite the evidence of the crisis, climate-displaced people are falling into a . The term “climate refugee”, widely used in the media, has no value in international law: the 1951 Geneva Convention protects people persecuted by their own State, but climate change is not the fault of any specific persecutor, it is a global phenomenon. [[legal vacuum]]

Without official status, these people do not benefit from the principle of , which prohibits sending someone back to a place where their life would be in danger. This lack of protection creates an injustice: the most affected countries have historically polluted the least, while rich countries often close their borders. Hence the idea of ​​a **climate debt**: the moral responsibility of industrialized countries towards populations made vulnerable by their own development. **[[non-refoulement]]**

Some countries are already looking for new solutions. Small island states are considering remaining a nation recognized by the UN even if their island has disappeared underwater. Kiribati, for example, purchased land in Fiji to prepare, if necessary, for the relocation of its entire population.

In 2018, the **Global Compact on Migration** began to discuss the environmental causes of departures. But the priority remains **local adaptation**: dykes, salt-resistant crops, warning systems, to allow people to stay at home as long as possible. Because the migration undergone always remains experienced as a failure, and massive and disorderly flows risk fueling tensions around water and habitable land.

In 2022, climate disasters will cause 60 million internal displacements, surpassing war refugees for the first time. Lacking a recognized legal status, these populations remain unprotected in the face of a crisis that could affect 216 million people by 2050.
